title: Class Field Theory
summary: This library studies abelian extensions of local fields, number fields, and global function fields through reciprocity, norm subgroups, and class fields.
overview: Class field theory asks how the abelian extensions of a field can be described using the field itself. For a nonarchimedean local field, reciprocity identifies Galois groups with quotients of the multiplicative group by norm subgroups, and the existence theorem says which subgroups arise. For number fields, ray class groups describe Frobenius automorphisms, while the idèle class group gives a single description of all finite abelian extensions.

These descriptions also constrain ramification, determine the least ray class modulus needed for an extension, and relate global norm equations to local tests. Over the rational numbers, the Kronecker–Weber theorem makes the extensions concrete by placing them in cyclotomic fields. The selected local reciprocity map and Hilbert pairing results assert existence without imposing additional normalization.

For global function fields over finite fields, the actual idèle norm gives an inclusion-reversing classification of finite abelian extensions by open subgroups of finite index. Completing the idèle class group gives the absolute abelian Galois group. The local and global Artin maps agree at each place, with arithmetic Frobenius giving the normalization at unramified places.
scopeNote: The selection covers local fields, number fields, and global function fields over finite fields. The function-field existence theorem uses the ordinary idèle-class topology; its local–global comparison concerns the actual constructed Artin maps. The selected local-field reciprocity and Hilbert-pairing results assert existence without imposing additional normalization.

entries.title: Local reciprocity for finite abelian extensions
entries.summary: A finite abelian extension is recovered as a quotient of the base field's multiplicative group by its norm subgroup.
statement: Let $K$ be a nonarchimedean local field, with its valuative topology, and let $L/K$ be a finite abelian Galois extension. There exists a continuous surjective homomorphism
$$\operatorname{Art}_{L/K}:K^\times\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(L/K),\qquad \ker(\operatorname{Art}_{L/K})=N_{L/K}(L^\times).$$
Here $N_{L/K}(L^\times)$ is the subgroup of field norms.
discussion: The norm subgroup tells precisely when two elements of the base field induce the same Galois automorphism. This turns questions about an extension into multiplicative arithmetic within the base field. Serre's Local Fields presents this finite form of reciprocity through the cohomological approach associated with Hochschild and Artin–Tate, providing a starting point for the broader local theory.
history: Serre's Local Fields presents the cohomological approach to local reciprocity, following the development associated with Hochschild and Artin–Tate. This finite quotient formulation is a convenient point of entry to that theory.

entries.title: Local reciprocity and the abelian absolute Galois group
entries.summary: All finite abelian local extensions fit into one topological isomorphism.
statement: For a nonarchimedean local field $K$, let $\widehat{K^\times}_{\mathrm{top}}$ be the inverse limit of $K^\times/U$ over open normal subgroups $U$ of finite index. Then
$$\widehat{K^\times}_{\mathrm{top}}\ \simeq_{\mathrm{top}}\ G_K^{\mathrm{ab}},\qquad G_K=\operatorname{Gal}(K^{\mathrm{sep}}/K).$$
The right side is the topological abelianization: the quotient by the closure of the commutator subgroup.
discussion: Passing to the inverse limit retains exactly the finite continuous quotients of the multiplicative group that matter for abelian Galois theory. The completion is therefore essential: it incorporates the topology while bringing all finite extensions into one description. Lubin and Tate's 1965 formal-group construction gives an explicit perspective on these extensions, complementary to the cohomological approach presented by Serre.
history: Lubin and Tate's 1965 paper supplies an explicit formal-group perspective on local abelian extensions. Serre's cohomological presentation gives a complementary route to the reciprocity theorem assembled here at the profinite level.

entries.title: Local class fields: classification by norm subgroups
entries.summary: Every open finite-index subgroup is a norm subgroup, with the correct reversal of inclusion.
statement: Fix a nonarchimedean local field $K$ and a separable closure. Finite abelian intermediate extensions correspond to open finite-index subgroups of $K^\times$ through
$$L\longmapsto N_{L/K}(L^\times).$$
The correspondence reverses inclusion: $L_1\subseteq L_2$ exactly when $N_{L_2/K}(L_2^\times)\subseteq N_{L_1/K}(L_1^\times)$.
discussion: Reciprocity associates a norm subgroup to an extension; the existence theorem supplies the converse and makes the classification complete. Larger extensions correspond to smaller subgroups, so inclusion questions become comparisons within the base field. This classical complement to reciprocity has an explicit construction through Lubin–Tate theory and is treated alongside local symbols in Serre's Local Fields.
history: The existence theorem complements reciprocity in classical local class field theory. Lubin–Tate theory provides explicit local abelian extensions, while Serre treats existence together with local symbols in the final part of Local Fields.

entries.title: Artin reciprocity for finite abelian number-field extensions
entries.summary: A ray class Artin map realizes Frobenius automorphisms in a finite abelian number-field extension.
statement: Let $L/K$ be a finite abelian extension of number fields. There are a modulus $\mathfrak m$ and a surjective homomorphism
$$\operatorname{Art}_{L/K,\mathfrak m}:\mathrm{Cl}_{\mathfrak m}(K)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(L/K).$$
Here $\mathrm{Cl}_{\mathfrak m}(K)$ is the ray class group of modulus $\mathfrak m$.

The extension is unramified away from $\mathfrak m$. For a finite prime $\mathfrak p$ outside its finite support and a prime $\mathfrak P$ above $\mathfrak p$, the map sends $[\mathfrak p]$ to the arithmetic Frobenius at $\mathfrak P$.
discussion: Away from the modulus, a prime's image under the Artin map records its Frobenius automorphism; an identity value means that the prime splits completely. Congruence conditions on ideals thus describe the behavior of primes in an extension. Artin's 1927 reciprocity map made the class-field correspondence canonical through Frobenius, building on the earlier work discussed in Milne's historical account.
history: Artin's 1927 reciprocity map made the correspondence with Galois groups canonical through Frobenius. Milne's historical discussion explains the earlier contributions of Kronecker, Weber, Hilbert, and Takagi to the class-field correspondence.

entries.title: Idelic reciprocity for number fields
entries.summary: The identity component is exactly the part removed from the idèle class group to obtain the abelian Galois group.
statement: Let $K$ be a number field, $\mathbb A_K^\times$ its idèle group, and $C_K=\mathbb A_K^\times/K^\times$ its idèle class group. Write $C_K^0$ for the connected component of the identity. Then
$$C_K/C_K^0\ \simeq_{\mathrm{top}}\ G_K^{\mathrm{ab}}.$$
Here $G_K=\operatorname{Gal}(K^{\mathrm{sep}}/K)$, and $G_K^{\mathrm{ab}}$ denotes its topological abelianization.
discussion: Idèle classes assemble multiplicative information from all completions of a number field. Removing the connected component leaves the group that records its finite abelian extensions, unifying finite-place and infinite-place conditions in one topological description. Milne presents this idelic formulation alongside ideal-theoretic reciprocity, within the algebraic and cohomological development associated with Chevalley and Artin–Tate.
history: Milne's notes explain the algebraic and cohomological approach associated with Chevalley and Artin–Tate and present both ideal-theoretic and idelic reciprocity. The idelic formulation unifies finite-place and infinite-place conditions.

entries.title: Hasse–Arf: integral ramification breaks
entries.summary: Upper ramification breaks of a finite abelian local extension are integral.
statement: Let $L/K$ be a finite abelian extension of nonarchimedean local fields, with compatible valuations. Let $G_i$ be the lower ramification groups, and put
$$\varphi(n)=\frac{1}{|G_0|}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|G_i|\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$
If $G_n\ne G_{n+1}$, then $\varphi(n)\in\mathbb Z$. The formal statement gives an integer $z$ with the rational equality $\varphi(n)=z$.
discussion: Upper numbering can take rational values, but its jumps in the abelian case occur at integers. This restriction on wild ramification underlies the integral conductor exponents of class field theory; nonabelian extensions can have fractional upper jumps. Arf's ramification paper appeared in 1940, and Serre's Local Fields develops the ramification and norm theory surrounding the Hasse–Arf theorem.
history: Arf's original ramification paper appeared in volume 181 of Crelle's journal in 1940. Serre's Local Fields develops the ramification and norm theory in which the Hasse–Arf theorem is situated.

entries.title: Existence of a perfect local Hilbert pairing
entries.summary: Power classes are dual to their roots-of-unity-valued characters.
statement: Let $K$ be a nonarchimedean local field, let $n>0$ be nonzero in $K$, and assume that $K$ contains a primitive $n$th root of unity. Set $P=K^\times/(K^\times)^n$. There exists a bimultiplicative pairing
$$B:P\times P\longrightarrow\mu_n(K),\qquad P\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\operatorname{Hom}(P,\mu_n(K)),\quad a\longmapsto B(a,-).$$

It is skew-symmetric, nondegenerate, and satisfies the Steinberg relation. For representatives $a,b\in K^\times$, one has $B([a],[b])=1$ exactly when $b$ is a norm from the Kummer algebra $K[T]/(T^n-a)$.
discussion: A nontrivial power class is detected by pairing it with a suitable second class, while a trivial pairing value expresses a norm condition. This turns local norm equations into orthogonality tests and connects Kummer extensions with multiplicative characters. These connections are the classical role of local norm-residue symbols, which Serre treats together with the existence theorem in Local Fields.
history: Local norm-residue symbols connect reciprocity with Kummer theory. Serre treats local symbols and the existence theorem together; the duality formulation explains how norm tests encode characters of power-class groups.

entries.title: The cyclic Hasse norm theorem
entries.summary: For a cyclic number-field extension, local norm equations have a global solution.
statement: Let $L/K$ be a finite cyclic Galois extension of number fields and let $a\in K^\times$. Then
$$a\in N_{L/K}(L^\times)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\in N_{L\otimes_K K_v\,/\,K_v}\bigl((L\otimes_K K_v)^\times\bigr)\ \text{for every place }v.$$
The right side includes every finite and every infinite completion. The norm after base change is the determinant norm of the resulting finite algebra.
discussion: The theorem makes a global multiplicative equation testable at every finite and infinite completion. Cyclicity is essential: for more general extensions, an obstruction can remain even when every local norm test succeeds. This is a classical example of the local-to-global principle, treated by Milne through cyclic cohomology and idèle classes together with the limitations of the noncyclic case.
history: The Hasse norm theorem is a central example of a local-to-global principle. Milne treats it through cyclic cohomology and idèle classes and explains why the corresponding assertion fails for general noncyclic extensions.

entries.title: The least ray class modulus of an abelian extension
entries.summary: A unique least modulus measures which ray class fields contain the extension.
statement: For a finite abelian extension $L/K$ of number fields, there is a unique ray class modulus $\mathfrak f$ such that, for every modulus $\mathfrak m$,
$$L\text{ embeds over }K\text{ in a ray class field for }\mathfrak m\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathfrak f\leq\mathfrak m.$$
The order compares the finite exponents and the allowed infinite part. Thus the conclusion specifies the whole upward-closed set of admissible moduli.
discussion: The conductor packages the congruence conditions needed to realize an extension as a class field. Its finite exponents measure ramification depth, while its infinite part records real places that become complex; comparison with this one modulus decides which ray class fields contain the extension. Ray class groups are the classical means of allowing ramification, developed with conductors in Milne's ideal-theoretic presentation.
history: Ray class groups are the classical mechanism for allowing ramification in class field theory. Milne develops moduli, conductors, and ray class fields together in the ideal-theoretic presentation of the global theory.

entries.title: The Kronecker–Weber theorem
entries.summary: Every finite abelian extension of the rational numbers embeds into a cyclotomic field.
statement: Every finite abelian extension $L/\mathbb Q$ is contained in a cyclotomic field. More precisely, there exist an integer $n>0$ and a $\mathbb Q$-algebra embedding
$$L\hookrightarrow\mathbb Q(\zeta_n),$$
where $\zeta_n$ is a primitive $n$th root of unity.
discussion: Roots of unity therefore suffice to generate fields containing every finite abelian extension of the rational numbers, and their union is the maximal abelian extension. This gives a concrete model for the broader problem of explicitly generating abelian extensions. As Milne recounts, Hilbert proved the theorem in 1896 after earlier incomplete proofs by Kronecker and Weber.
history: Milne records Hilbert's 1896 proof following earlier incomplete proofs by Kronecker and Weber. The theorem is the rational-number-field prototype for the broader problem of explicitly generating abelian extensions.

entries.title: Class field theory for global function fields
entries.summary: Open subgroups of finite index in the ordinary idèle class group classify finite abelian extensions, and completion gives absolute reciprocity.
statement: Let $k$ be a finite field and $K/k$ a function field finite over a chosen $k(t)$. Write $C_K=\mathbb A_K^\times/K^\times$ with its ordinary quotient topology. Every open subgroup $H\subseteq C_K$ of finite index is exactly $N_{L/K}(C_L)$ for a unique finite abelian extension $L/K$ inside a fixed separable closure.
The actual norm map supplies an inclusion-reversing equivalence $L\longmapsto N_{L/K}(C_L)$. The constructed finite Artin map and the completed absolute Artin map give
$$C_K/N_{L/K}(C_L)\simeq\operatorname{Gal}(L/K),\qquad \widehat{C_K}\xrightarrow{\sim}G_K^{\mathrm{ab}}.$$

The completion uses all ordinary open subgroups of finite index, and the second isomorphism is an isomorphism of topological groups extending the constructed absolute Artin map. Norm cofinality is proved, rather than supplied as an existence hypothesis.

The Lean interface uses principal-divisor data: every nonzero function has a finitely supported divisor of valuation orders and degree zero. The library constructs these data from the function-field structure over the finite base field, and for its finite extensions.
discussion: This is an existence and classification theorem: an open finite-index subgroup actually produces its class field. The same norm subgroups also determine the topology needed for completed reciprocity, so the finite classification and the absolute Galois description fit together.

The kernel is the image of the field extension’s idèle norm. This makes the correspondence usable for comparing concrete extensions and for recovering an extension from its norm subgroup. Milne’s Arithmetic Duality Theorems treats the function-field version in Chapter I, Appendix A.
history: Function-field class field theory expresses abelian covering data through idèles and their norm groups. Milne’s Chapter I, Appendix A develops its local and global reciprocity formulations.

entries.title: Local–global compatibility of function-field Artin maps
entries.summary: The actual local Artin map agrees with global reciprocity on a one-place idèle and has the arithmetic Frobenius normalization.
statement: Let $L/K$ be a finite abelian extension of global function fields over a finite field $k$, with compatible rational-parameter structures and principal-divisor data. Let $w$ be a place of $L$ above $v$ of $K$. For $x\in K_v^\times$, write $[x]_v\in C_K$ for the class of the idèle equal to $x$ at $v$ and $1$ elsewhere. Then
$$\operatorname{Art}_{w}(x)=\operatorname{Art}_{L/K}([x]_v)\quad\text{in }\operatorname{Gal}(L/K).$$
If the ramification index at $w$ is $1$, the decomposition-group Artin map satisfies
$$\operatorname{Art}^{D_w}_{w}(x)=\operatorname{Frob}_w^{\operatorname{ord}_v(x)}.$$

Here $\operatorname{Frob}_w$ induces $y\mapsto y^{\#\kappa(v)}$ on the residue field. In particular a uniformizer maps to arithmetic Frobenius, and local units map to the identity in the unramified case.
discussion: The comparison identifies the independently constructed local and global maps. It permits a global Artin value to be calculated place by place and fixes the Frobenius convention through its residue-field action.

The unramified formula provides a concrete calculation for every local element, including its valuation and unit part. Local reciprocity and the expression of global reciprocity through local maps are developed together in Milne’s function-field appendix.
history: Milne’s Arithmetic Duality Theorems, Chapter I, Appendix A presents local reciprocity with the arithmetic Frobenius convention and its relation to global reciprocity.
